title: The Girl Who Was Mailed To Grandma
sources: History.com, 'When Americans Mailed Their Children' (parcel post began January 1, 1913; in February 1914 May Pierstorff, nearly six, was mailed 73 miles from Grangeville to her grandparents in Lewiston, Idaho, for 53 cents in stamps attached to her coat; a relative who was a postal worker took her on a Railway Mail train; the Postmaster General then banned accepting people as mail)

Wikipedia, 'Charlotte May Pierstorff' (48.5 pounds; rode in the mail car with Leonard Mochel, her mother's cousin, a railway postal clerk, who delivered her to her grandmother; the case led to rules against mailing people; day-old poultry stayed mailable)
USPS Publication 52 / DMM 526: day-old poultry (live baby chicks) can still be mailed today
Parcel post weight limit was raised to 50 pounds for the first and second zones on January 1, 1914

lines.text: In 1914, a couple in Idaho mailed their five year old daughter
lines.caps: In 1914, | a couple | in Idaho | mailed | their | five year old | daughter

lines.text: to her grandma's house.
With the stamps stuck right on her coat.
See, the post office had just started delivering packages,
and May's parents wanted her to visit grandma,
seventy-three miles away.
But a train ticket wasn't cheap.
So her dad walked her into the post office
and asked how much it costs to mail a kid.
The clerk checked the rules,
and nothing said he couldn't.
May weighed forty-eight and a half pounds,
lines.caps: May | weighed | 48 and a half | pounds,

lines.text: just under the fifty pound limit.
So on went fifty-three cents in stamps,
lines.caps: So on | went | 53 cents | in stamps,

lines.text: and she rode the train in the mail car,
with her mom's cousin, who happened to be the mail clerk.
He walked her right up to grandma's front door.
Soon after, the post office banned mailing people.
Which is why today, you can still mail baby chicks,
but not your little sister.
